title: One studio or split design and development
metaTitle: One studio or a split team
excerpt: One team should design and build when the site has to look like the decisions. Splitting the work adds a translation step that drops the hard parts.
alt: A wide mountain valley with snowy peaks, a braided river, and evergreen trees in the foreground, one landscape held together rather than assembled later.
caption: A valley read as one landscape. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What gets lost when design and development are split?
faqs.answer: The handoff usually drops empty and error states, the priority of the page, real mobile behavior, and the words that were doing the work. Color is easy to write down. Behavior is what the second team has to invent.

faqs.question: When is a split still reasonable?
faqs.answer: A split can work when a stable design system already exists and your own engineers know how to ship pages, or when the extra partner is a specialist on a narrow edge such as payments. It is a poor fit when the file is only a homepage and a mood, and the interface itself is the risk.

faqs.question: What should you own at the end of a one-team project?
faqs.answer: You should have the design file, the repository, the hosting accounts in your name, and a place for brand files and notes after launch. Ask who will change the component when it looks wrong on a phone. If the answer is two companies, you are buying a split.

markdown:
A design and development studio is the better fit when the site or the product has to look like the decisions, not like a handoff. Splitting design and development adds a translation step. Someone has to explain the frames to someone who was not in the room, and the interface becomes a reconstruction.

One team is not a moral position. It is a way to keep the decisions intact until they are in the browser. If your project can survive a careful handoff, a split can be the right staffing. Most early product sites survive it worse than founders expect.

## The translation step

Design produces a set of decisions: what the first screen says, what the component does when it is empty, what happens on a phone, what the type is allowed to do. Development produces a site. The translation step is the document, the meeting, or the ticket in which those decisions move from one group to the other.

Every translation drops something. The dropped thing is rarely the color. Color is written down. The dropped thing is the behavior: which part is the offer, which animation is optional, which empty state is honest, which line of copy is doing the real work. A developer who was not in the critique will implement the frame they were given. The frame was one state.

You can reduce the loss with a better file. You cannot reduce it to zero. Specs help. Redlines help. A recorded walkthrough helps. They are all still a retelling. The person who made the tradeoff is the fastest person to apply it when the browser disagrees with the frame, and the browser will disagree.

This is why the split feels efficient on a plan and expensive in the last two weeks. The plan shows two workstreams. The last two weeks show a queue of questions. "What should this do on a small phone?" "Is this line allowed to wrap?" "The illustration is a megabyte." Those questions are the translation step presenting its bill.

## What the handoff usually drops

A few categories cover most of the damage.

- Empty, error, and loading states. The design file shows the happy path. The build has to show the others. A team that was not in the room invents them, and the inventions sound like a different product.
- The priority of the page. If everything in the file looks equally polished, everything gets built to the same depth. The offer should have been first.
- Responsive behavior that was waved through. A desktop frame scaled down is not a mobile page. The handoff often says "make it work on mobile" and calls that a specification.
- Performance. A frame does not show weight. The photograph, the font, the motion, and the script are decisions. If they are made after the file is "done," they are made under pressure, and the page gets heavy.
- The sentence. Copy in a frame is often placeholder that became permanent because nobody owned the words across the seam.

None of these require a villain. They require two backlogs. Each side finishes its backlog. The seam is nobody's backlog until the site is about to launch.

A single team still has arguments. The arguments happen before the thing is built twice. The designer and the engineer look at the same Next.js page, in React and TypeScript, and change the component. Tailwind makes the styling visible in the same place. Motion, if you use it, is in the component, not in a prototype that will be approximated later. The loop is shorter because there is no seam to cross.

## When a split is reasonable

Split the work when the seam is small and the translator is strong. A marketing site with a stable design system, handed to an in-house engineering team that has shipped pages before, can work. The system is the translator. Components already exist. The design is a new arrangement, not a new physics.

Split when you truly need a specialist the studio does not have, and the interface is not the risk. A security review, a payments integration, a data migration: those can be another firm, with a clear edge. The visual and front-end decisions can still sit with one team. Do not split the interface itself into "looks" and "behavior" if you can help it. That is the expensive seam.

Split when the design is already done, it is thorough, and you are only building. "Thorough" means states, mobile, type, empty cases, and the actual words. If the file is a homepage and a vibe, you are not ready for a build-only contract. You will pay the translator during the build, at a worse time.

A split can also be a way to use people you already employ. If you have engineers and you lack design, hire design and keep the build. If you have a designer and a capable front-end engineer, you may not need a studio at all. The studio is how you rent the pair when you do not have it inside.

## When one team should hold it

Hold design and build together when the product is the interface. Got Next and Leadly are public examples of product interface work. The decisions are things like what a person sees first and how a flow feels in the hand. Those decisions die in translation. They need the person who argued for them to be present when the component is stubborn.

Hold them together when the schedule is short enough that a handoff would consume the calendar. A conference page, a launch, a replacement for a site that is wrong in public: you do not have time for a second interpretation. One sequence, from the sentence to the deploy.

Hold them together when you want one conversation. Founders get tired of explaining the offer twice, once to design and once to engineering, and then again when the two summaries disagree. A single studio conversation is not automatically better. It is better when that studio actually builds, and when the people in the room are the people who will touch the code. A studio that designs and then subcontracts the build has recreated the seam and added a margin.

Hanabi designs and builds. The production stack is Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, and Motion where motion earns its place, deployed on Vercel. That is the practical meaning of one team here. The design tools are Figma, Framer, and Illustrator. The files are not a separate deliverable that disappears over a wall. They are how the build stays inspectable.

## Files, code, and the record

One team still owes you a record. You should leave with the Figma file, the repository, the accounts in your name, and a place the brand files and project notes remain after launch. The client portal exists for that: brand files, docs, and updates, so the work is not trapped in someone's inbox.

Ask, before you hire, who writes the component and who will be in the review when it looks wrong on a phone. If the answer is two companies, you are buying a split, whatever the proposal calls it. If the answer is one group that can change the frame and the code in the same week, you are buying the shorter loop.

[Google's people-first content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether a page demonstrates first-hand knowledge, the kind that comes from having actually used the thing you are describing. The sentences on a marketing site are that kind of page. They should come from people who understand the offer, and they survive better when the same people can change the interface that carries them. A visitor can feel a chain of retellings. It shows up as a page that looks assembled, and as copy that could belong to a neighboring company.

Bring the moving decisions to the first working session, in a list, not in a slide. Include the sentence you are still unsure of, the screen that does not exist yet, and the state you hope nobody hits. A split team will turn that list into tickets. One team will turn it into the page. Either way the list is the scope. If you cannot write it, you are not ready to hire a build-only partner, and you may not be ready to hire a studio either. The list is the work.

Write the scope so the responsibility is unbroken. "Design and build the marketing site" is one scope. "Deliver a Figma file" and, later, "implement this Figma file" are two scopes. Both can be valid contracts. They are not the same project, and the second one needs a much better file.

## How to choose

List the decisions that will still be moving during the build. If the list is long, keep one team, because those decisions will be made in the code whether you plan for it or not. If the list is short and your engineers already know the system, a design partner plus your team can be enough.

Name the seam in the proposal if you do split. Who attends the build reviews. How many rounds of correction are included. What happens when the browser cannot match the frame. A split with a named seam is a professional arrangement. A split with a vague "collaboration" is a hope.

Either path can end in a fixed launch or an ongoing relationship. The next choice is how you buy the time: a bounded launch, or a retainer with the same people while the product keeps moving. That piece is [retainer or a fixed launch](/blog/retainer-or-a-fixed-launch).

If you want one team for the design and the build, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min).
